rows.verified: Chainsaws can cause fatal or major injuries if used incorrectly, so operators must be competent for the type of work undertaken.
Chainsaw operators at work must receive adequate training relevant to their tasks.
Operators are required to wear appropriate chainsaw protective clothing whenever using a chainsaw.
Safe chainsaw management includes fitness to operate, equipment selection, maintenance, lone-working arrangements and first aid.
Task-appropriate chainsaw PPE can include head, hearing, eye, hand, leg and foot protection.
Tree climbing with personal fall-protection systems requires task-specific training and rescue competence.
Forestry and arboriculture work must control public access with suitable signs, barriers, diversions or additional personnel where needed.
HSE investigations identify shortcuts and failure to follow good practice as recurring factors in fatal and major chainsaw injuries.
Chainsaw risk depends on saw type, task, timber, terrain, weather, operator competence, PPE, maintenance and emergency arrangements.
HSE chainsaw evidence is operator-, task-, equipment-, site-, control- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury probability.
Livestock work requires proper handling facilities kept in good working order.
Cattle-handling systems should include a suitable race and crush for the animals handled.
Livestock handlers should be trained and competent, with a rigorous policy for temperamental animals.
Cattle handling exposes people to crushing, kicking, butting and goring hazards.
Working on unrestrained cattle or using makeshift equipment is particularly hazardous.
A cattle crush should provide effective head and rump restraint, secure anchoring, safe access and a slip-resistant floor.
No person should enter a bull enclosure while the bull is loose.
Sheep handling should use races or turnover crates, while pig handling should use pig boards and suitable restraint or segregation.
Livestock risk depends on species, temperament, handling frequency, facilities, restraint, worker competence, visitors and task conditions.
HSE livestock evidence is animal-, facility-, worker-, task-, control- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury probability.
